results.question: What is CUDA?
results.response:
CUDA (Compute Unified Device Architecture) is NVIDIA’s parallel computing platform and programming model that lets software run on NVIDIA GPUs for high-performance computing and accelerated workloads (most commonly, AI/deep learning). It provides the development stack (e.g., CUDA C/C++ and libraries) and the runtime/driver support to let programmers write kernels that execute massively parallel work on the GPU, while the CPU coordinates data movement and kernel launches.

Background (general NVIDIA knowledge): CUDA is the foundation for NVIDIA’s GPU acceleration ecosystem; many AI frameworks and GPU-accelerated libraries use CUDA under the hood to achieve performance.

results.question: How do tensor cores work?
results.response:
Tensor Cores are specialized units on NVIDIA GPUs that accelerate **matrix multiply-accumulate (MMA)** operations (the core math behind neural networks). Instead of computing a large dot product with many scalar floating-point instructions, the Tensor Core takes **tiles (blocks) of matrices**—commonly **FP16/BF16/FP8** (and also FP32/FP64 in newer modes)—and performs an MMA operation internally much more efficiently.

On GPUs like Ampere (example: A100), NVIDIA describes this at the instruction level: **a single Tensor Core “DMMA” job replaces multiple traditional FP64 instructions** (e.g., “one computer instruction” standing in for “eight traditional FP64 instructions”) by using matrix-math hardware designed for these MMA patterns. In practice, CUDA libraries (e.g., WMMA/CUDA Tensor Core APIs) break your workload into the right matrix tile shapes and feed them to Tensor Cores; software features like Hopper’s **Transformer Engine** then further optimize precision and data movement to keep Tensor Cores busy and boost throughput.

**Background (general NVIDIA knowledge):** Tensor Cores expect dense linear algebra expressed as batched GEMM/GEMM; they rely on warps and MMA instruction scheduling to stream matrix fragments through the hardware. You typically get the biggest gains when the model/layers can be represented in the supported precisions (FP16/BF16/FP8) and the kernel uses the Tensor Core code paths.

Sources:  
[1] What Is a Double-Precision Tensor Core? | NVIDIA Blog - https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/double-precision-tensor-cores/  
[2] H100 Transformer Engine Supercharges AI Training, Delivering Up to 6x Higher Performance Without Losing Accuracy | NVIDIA Blog - https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/h100-transformer-engine/  
[3] What Is Sparsity in AI Inference and Machine Learning? | NVIDIA Blog - https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/sparsity-ai-inference/

results.question: What is TensorRT?
results.response:

results.question: How does DLSS work?
results.response:
DLSS (Deep Learning Super Sampling) works by using an NVIDIA-trained AI model to **reconstruct a higher-resolution image** from what the game originally renders at a lower resolution. In general, the GPU takes **low-res frames** plus **frame-to-frame motion information** (e.g., motion vectors/optical-flow-style data, depending on the DLSS version) and the Tensor Cores run the network to generate a sharper, more detailed output than conventional upscaling. For DLSS 3 specifically, NVIDIA describes it as an **AI-powered upscaling approach on RTX 40-series hardware** that’s designed to improve real-time rendering performance (often discussed alongside path tracing and latency considerations).  

Background (general NVIDIA knowledge): DLSS is implemented as a per-game/per-resolution “AI upscaling” pipeline where the model is trained offline and then executed in real time on the GPU; the model uses both the rendered image content and temporal signals to reduce aliasing (“jaggies”) and improve detail recovery.
